title: Testing and debugging functions
goals: Design revealing tests for a function
Repair a defect and rerun earlier cases

prerequisite.prompt: For capacity 9 and used 2, what should remaining return?

vocabulary: An edge of a permitted range
A previously working case that fails after a change
A check that raises an error when its condition is false

blocks.text: A function can pass one example by coincidence. Start with a written rule, calculate expected results independently, and include ordinary, zero and boundary cases. We will test a subtraction function under the contract 0 <= used <= capacity.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: Each parenthesized group is a tuple, an ordered group of values. The loop unpacks each group into three names. Equality compares the actual result to the independently calculated expected result. The worked script prints True three times. An assert actual == expected could instead stop at the first mismatch with AssertionError.

blocks.label: Would replacing the body with return 5 pass every worked case? Identify the first revealing test.

blocks.text: A faulty return capacity + used gives 11, 16 and 8. The unused case passes even though the rule is wrong. Repair the operator to subtraction and rerun all three cases. Never change an expected result merely to match faulty output.

Passing this small suite supports these particular cases. It neither proves every allowed input correct nor checks invalid input handling. A test outside the contract needs a separately specified expected behavior.

workbook.title: Write expectations
workbook.prompt: Give expected results for remaining(6, 2), remaining(6, 6) and remaining(6, 0).

workbook.title: Find a revealing case
workbook.prompt: A faulty function always returns 4. Which of your three cases pass and fail?
workbook.answer: Only (6, 2) passes. The full and unused cases fail.

workbook.title: Repair and retest
workbook.prompt: A faulty function adds capacity and used. For (6, 2), state actual and expected. Repair it and name a regression case.
workbook.answer: Actual 8, expected 4. Subtract used; rerun a prior case such as (6, 0), expecting 6.

workbook.title: Test a new function independently
workbook.prompt: Define stock(packs, loose) to return packs * 4 + loose. Create expected tests for (2, 3), (0, 3), (2, 0), then show which detects a faulty packs + loose body.
workbook.answer: Expected 11, 3, 8. Faulty results 5, 3, 2; first and third reveal it. Use independent expectations in the test loop.

workbook.title: Limit the conclusion
workbook.prompt: All three stock tests pass. Does that prove correct handling of negative counts?
workbook.answer: No. Negative counts are outside our nonnegative-input contract and were not tested; rejection behavior must first be defined.

teacher.background: Teach Week 12 as a two-session investigation using fictional data. A function can pass one example by coincidence. Start with a written rule, calculate expected results independently, and include ordinary, zero and boundary cases. We will test a subtraction function under the contract 0 <= used <= capacity. Assess the three stated outcomes through the independent task, not by copying the worked result.
materials: Python 3 editor with a fresh local practice file
Paper trace table and the student workbook
Fictional input records from this lesson; no real student identifiers
sessions: Retrieve the prerequisite and explain the purpose in the opening section.
Read the worked example and diagram; ask learners to trace each step aloud.
Complete W1 and W2, then compare predictions with observed results.
Collect the guided prediction before running; discuss a mismatch and its cause.
Retrieve the main rule without showing the previous answer.
Use W3 to diagnose and repair the stated failure; rerun an earlier case.
Collect W4 independently, including code or plan, predictions and explanations, before hints.
Discuss W5 and the exit; use the fresh retry when support was needed.
